chapter_text:
CHAPTER 27 - METALS AND NON-METALS

Introduction

All around us we find materials made of different elements. Of the more than 100 known elements, the majority are metals (such as iron, copper, aluminium, gold and sodium), while a smaller number are non-metals (such as oxygen, carbon, sulphur, chlorine and nitrogen). A few elements that show properties of both are called metalloids (for example silicon and germanium). In this chapter we study the physical and chemical properties that distinguish metals from non-metals, the reactivity series, how metals occur in nature and are extracted (metallurgy), why and how metals corrode, and the useful mixtures we make from metals called alloys.

27.1 PHYSICAL PROPERTIES OF METALS

Metals share a set of characteristic physical properties:
 - Metallic lustre: freshly cut metals have a shiny surface. Example: silver, gold.
 - Malleability: metals can be beaten into thin sheets without breaking. Gold and silver are the most malleable; aluminium foil is a common example.
 - Ductility: metals can be drawn into thin wires. Copper and aluminium wires are everyday examples.
 - Conductivity: metals are good conductors of heat and electricity. Silver and copper are the best conductors of electricity.
 - Sonority: metals make a ringing sound when struck (used in bells).
 - High melting and boiling points: most metals are solids with high melting points (iron melts at about 1538 degrees C).
 - Density and strength: most metals are hard, strong and dense.
Metals are usually solid at room temperature.

27.2 PHYSICAL PROPERTIES OF NON-METALS

Non-metals generally show the opposite properties:
 - They are non-lustrous (dull), except graphite and iodine which are lustrous.
 - They are non-malleable and non-ductile - they are brittle in the solid state (for example sulphur and coal break into pieces when hammered).
 - They are poor conductors of heat and electricity (insulators), except graphite which conducts.
 - They have low melting and boiling points (except diamond).
 - They are not sonorous.
 - They occur as solids, liquids or gases (carbon, sulphur are solids; bromine is a liquid; oxygen, nitrogen, chlorine are gases).

27.3 EXCEPTIONS TO REMEMBER

Some elements break the general rules and are commonly asked in examinations:
 - Mercury is a metal but is LIQUID at room temperature.
 - Sodium and potassium are metals but are so SOFT that they can be cut with a knife.
 - Graphite is a non-metal (a form of carbon) but is a good CONDUCTOR of electricity.
 - Diamond is a non-metal (a form of carbon) but is the HARDEST natural substance and has a very high melting point.
 - Iodine is a non-metal but is LUSTROUS (shiny).
 - Carbon (diamond) and silicon are non-metals with very high melting points.

27.4 CHEMICAL PROPERTIES OF METALS

(a) Reaction with oxygen -> basic oxides.
Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides, which are generally BASIC in nature.
   2 Mg + O2 -> 2 MgO
   4 Al + 3 O2 -> 2 Al2O3
   2 Cu + O2 -> 2 CuO
Metal oxides dissolve in water to give bases (alkalis): Na2O + H2O -> 2 NaOH. Some metal oxides such as Al2O3 and ZnO are AMPHOTERIC - they react with both acids and bases.

(b) Reaction with water.
Reactivity towards water varies:
 - Very reactive metals (sodium, potassium) react VIOLENTLY with cold water:
     2 Na + 2 H2O -> 2 NaOH + H2 (gas)
 - Calcium and magnesium react less vigorously.
 - Iron reacts with steam: 3 Fe + 4 H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4 H2.
 - Metals like copper, silver and gold do NOT react with water.

(c) Reaction with dilute acids -> hydrogen gas.
Metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series displace hydrogen from dilute acids:
   Zn + 2 HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2
   Mg + H2SO4 -> MgSO4 + H2
Copper, silver and gold do NOT react with dilute HCl or H2SO4 because they are below hydrogen in the reactivity series.

(d) Reaction with salt solutions - displacement.
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution:
   Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu (iron displaces copper; blue colour fades and a reddish-brown deposit forms on the iron)
   Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu

27.5 IONIC (ELECTROVALENT) BONDING - A RECAP

Metals lose electrons to form positive ions (cations); non-metals gain electrons to form negative ions (anions). The electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions is the IONIC BOND. For example, sodium (2,8,1) loses one electron to become Na+ and chlorine (2,8,7) gains one electron to become Cl-, giving sodium chloride NaCl. Ionic compounds have high melting points, are usually soluble in water and conduct electricity when molten or dissolved.

27.6 CHEMICAL PROPERTIES OF NON-METALS

Non-metals react with oxygen to form oxides that are ACIDIC (or neutral). For example:
   C + O2 -> CO2 (carbon dioxide; CO2 + H2O -> H2CO3, carbonic acid)
   S + O2 -> SO2 (sulphur dioxide; SO2 + H2O -> H2SO3, sulphurous acid)
So non-metallic oxides turn blue litmus red (acidic), while metallic oxides turn red litmus blue (basic). Non-metals generally do not react with dilute acids and do not displace hydrogen, because they themselves tend to gain electrons rather than lose them.

27.7 REACTIVITY SERIES AND DISPLACEMENT REACTIONS

The REACTIVITY SERIES (activity series) is a list of metals arranged in decreasing order of reactivity. A common order (most reactive at the top) is:
   K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > (H) > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au
Potassium and sodium are the most reactive; gold and platinum are the least reactive (noble metals). Hydrogen is included as a reference: metals above hydrogen displace H2 from dilute acids; metals below hydrogen do not.
DISPLACEMENT: a metal higher in the series displaces one lower from its compounds. This explains why iron displaces copper from copper sulphate, but copper cannot displace iron from iron sulphate. The reactivity series guides the method used to extract each metal.

27.8 METALLURGY - OCCURRENCE AND EXTRACTION OF METALS

Occurrence: a few unreactive metals (gold, silver, platinum) occur FREE (native) in nature. Most metals occur combined as compounds. The naturally occurring compounds of metals are called MINERALS. A mineral from which a metal can be extracted PROFITABLY and conveniently is called an ORE. Common ores include haematite (Fe2O3) for iron, bauxite (Al2O3.2H2O) for aluminium and zinc blende (ZnS) for zinc.
The science of extracting metals from their ores and refining them is called METALLURGY.

Steps in the extraction of a metal:
 1. CONCENTRATION (enrichment) of the ore: removing earthy impurities (gangue). Methods include hand-picking, washing (gravity separation), magnetic separation and froth flotation.
 2. CONVERSION OF THE CONCENTRATED ORE TO ITS OXIDE:
    - ROASTING: heating a sulphide ore strongly in the presence of air. Example: 2 ZnS + 3 O2 -> 2 ZnO + 2 SO2.
    - CALCINATION: heating a carbonate ore strongly in the ABSENCE (or limited supply) of air. Example: ZnCO3 -> ZnO + CO2.
 3. REDUCTION OF THE OXIDE TO THE METAL:
    - Oxides of moderately reactive metals (Zn, Fe, Pb) are reduced by heating with a reducing agent such as carbon (coke): ZnO + C -> Zn + CO; Fe2O3 + 3 CO -> 2 Fe + 3 CO2.
    - Oxides of highly reactive metals (Na, Ca, Mg, Al) cannot be reduced by carbon; they are extracted by ELECTROLYSIS of their molten compounds (for example, aluminium from molten Al2O3 in the Hall-Heroult process; sodium from molten NaCl).
    - Unreactive metals (Hg, Cu found as sulphides) can be obtained by simply heating their ores: 2 HgS + 3 O2 -> 2 HgO + 2 SO2, then 2 HgO -> 2 Hg + O2.
 4. REFINING (purification): the impure metal is purified, most commonly by ELECTROLYTIC REFINING. The impure metal is made the ANODE and a thin strip of pure metal the CATHODE in a bath of a salt of the metal; pure metal deposits on the cathode while impurities settle below the anode as 'anode mud'.

Extraction summary by reactivity:
 - High reactivity (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al): electrolysis of molten ore.
 - Medium reactivity (Zn, Fe, Pb): roasting/calcination to the oxide, then reduction with carbon.
 - Low reactivity (Cu, Hg, Ag, Au): often found native or obtained by simple heating of the ore.

27.9 CORROSION

CORROSION is the slow eating away of a metal surface by the action of air, moisture or chemicals around it. The most familiar example is the RUSTING of iron, in which iron forms a reddish-brown flaky layer of hydrated iron(III) oxide (Fe2O3.xH2O).
Conditions necessary for rusting: BOTH air (oxygen) AND moisture (water) must be present. Iron does not rust in dry air alone or in water that is free of dissolved oxygen; the presence of salts and acids speeds up rusting.
Other examples: silver tarnishes (black coating of silver sulphide), copper develops a green coating (basic copper carbonate).
Prevention of corrosion:
 - Painting, greasing or oiling the surface to keep out air and moisture.
 - GALVANISING: coating iron with a layer of zinc; the zinc protects the iron even if scratched.
 - Electroplating with a less reactive metal (chromium, tin, nickel).
 - ALLOYING: converting iron into stainless steel (iron + chromium + nickel) which does not rust.

27.10 ALLOYS

An ALLOY is a homogeneous mixture of a metal with one or more other metals or non-metals. Alloys are made to improve properties such as strength, hardness, resistance to corrosion, lustre and lower melting point. Common alloys:
 - Brass: copper + zinc. Stronger and more lustrous than copper; used in utensils and decorative items.
 - Bronze: copper + tin. Hard and tough; used for statues, medals and bells.
 - Steel: iron + a small amount of carbon. Much harder and stronger than pure iron.
 - Stainless steel: iron + chromium + nickel + carbon. Resists rusting; used in cutlery and utensils.
 - Amalgam: an alloy of mercury with another metal (for example dental amalgam).
 - Solder: lead + tin (low melting point); used for joining (soldering) electrical wires.
Advantages of alloys: they are usually harder and stronger, more resistant to corrosion, and can have a lower melting point or a more attractive appearance than the pure metals.

SUMMARY

 - Metals are lustrous, malleable, ductile, sonorous, good conductors with high melting points; non-metals are generally dull, brittle, poor conductors with low melting points.
 - Exceptions: mercury (liquid metal), sodium (soft metal), graphite (conducting non-metal), diamond (hardest non-metal), iodine (lustrous non-metal).
 - Metals form basic oxides, react with water and dilute acids (releasing H2), and undergo displacement reactions; non-metals form acidic oxides.
 - The reactivity series (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, H, Cu, Hg, Ag, Au) predicts displacement and the method of extraction.
 - Metallurgy: concentration of ore, roasting/calcination to the oxide, reduction (carbon for medium reactivity, electrolysis for high reactivity), and refining (electrolytic refining).
 - Corrosion (rusting of iron needs air + moisture) is prevented by painting, galvanising, electroplating and alloying.
 - Alloys (brass, bronze, steel, stainless steel, amalgam, solder) are mixtures with improved properties.

chapter_summary.title: Metals and Non-metals - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Class 10 Science & Technology (212) summary for Lesson 27 compares the physical and chemical properties of metals and non-metals, introduces the reactivity series and displacement reactions, outlines the metallurgy used to extract metals from their ores, and explains corrosion, its prevention, and the alloys we make from metals.

details: Metals: lustrous, malleable, ductile, sonorous, conducting
Non-metals: dull, brittle, insulating, low m.p.
Exceptions: Hg liquid, Na soft, graphite conducts, diamond hardest, iodine lustrous

Metals above H displace H2 from acids

sections.heading: Physical properties and exceptions
bullets: Metals are lustrous, malleable (beaten into sheets), ductile (drawn into wires), sonorous, good conductors of heat and electricity, and have high melting points.
Non-metals are generally dull, brittle (not malleable or ductile), poor conductors, with low melting points, and may be solid, liquid or gas.
Key exceptions: mercury is a liquid metal; sodium and potassium are soft metals; graphite is a non-metal that conducts; diamond is the hardest non-metal; iodine is a lustrous non-metal.

sections.heading: Chemical properties
bullets: Metals react with oxygen to form basic oxides (2 Mg + O2 -> 2 MgO); some oxides like Al2O3 and ZnO are amphoteric.
Reactive metals react with water (2 Na + 2 H2O -> 2 NaOH + H2) and with dilute acids to release hydrogen (Zn + 2 HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2).
Non-metals react with oxygen to form acidic oxides (C + O2 -> CO2; S + O2 -> SO2) that turn blue litmus red.
In ionic bonding a metal loses electrons (forming a cation) and a non-metal gains them (forming an anion), e.g. Na+ and Cl- in NaCl.

sections.heading: Reactivity series and displacement
bullets: The reactivity series arranges metals in decreasing order of reactivity: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > (H) > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au.
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution: Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu.
Metals above hydrogen in the series displace H2 from dilute acids; metals below hydrogen (Cu, Ag, Au) do not.

sections.heading: Metallurgy - extraction of metals
bullets: Minerals are naturally occurring compounds of metals; an ore is a mineral from which a metal can be extracted profitably.
Extraction steps: concentration of the ore, conversion to the oxide by roasting (sulphides) or calcination (carbonates), reduction to the metal, and refining.

Highly reactive metals (Na, Ca, Mg, Al) are extracted by electrolysis of their molten ores; medium-reactivity metals (Zn, Fe, Pb) by reduction of the oxide with carbon; low-reactivity metals (Cu, Hg, Ag, Au) by simple heating or found native.
Impure metals are commonly purified by electrolytic refining (impure metal anode, pure metal cathode).

sections.heading: Corrosion and alloys
bullets: Corrosion is the slow eating away of a metal by air, moisture or chemicals; rusting of iron (hydrated Fe2O3) needs BOTH air and moisture.
Corrosion is prevented by painting/oiling, galvanising (zinc coating), electroplating and alloying (stainless steel).

An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of a metal with other metals or non-metals - examples are brass (Cu+Zn), bronze (Cu+Sn), steel (Fe+C), stainless steel (Fe+Cr+Ni), amalgam (with Hg) and solder (Pb+Sn).
Alloys are made because they are harder, stronger, more corrosion-resistant or more attractive than the pure metals.

key_takeaways: Metals are lustrous, malleable, ductile, sonorous and good conductors with high melting points; non-metals are mostly dull, brittle, insulating and low-melting.
Remember the exceptions: mercury (liquid metal), sodium (soft metal), graphite (conducting non-metal), diamond (hardest non-metal), iodine (lustrous non-metal).
Metals form basic oxides, release hydrogen with dilute acids, and undergo displacement; non-metals form acidic oxides.
The reactivity series K..Au predicts displacement reactions and the method of extraction of each metal.
Metallurgy involves concentration of the ore, roasting/calcination, reduction (carbon or electrolysis) and refining.
Rusting of iron requires both air and moisture and is prevented by painting, galvanising, electroplating and alloying.
Alloys such as brass, bronze, steel, stainless steel, amalgam and solder have improved properties over the pure metals.

glossary.definition: An element that is typically lustrous, malleable, ductile, sonorous and a good conductor of heat and electricity, and tends to lose electrons to form positive ions.
An element that is generally dull, brittle and a poor conductor, with a low melting point, and tends to gain electrons to form negative ions.
An element showing properties of both metals and non-metals, such as silicon and germanium.
The property of a metal by which it can be beaten into thin sheets without breaking.
The property of a metal by which it can be drawn into thin wires.
The property by which a metal produces a ringing sound when struck.
A metal oxide such as Al2O3 or ZnO that reacts with both acids and bases.
A list of metals arranged in decreasing order of chemical reactivity, used to predict displacement reactions and methods of extraction.
A reaction in which a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution or compound.
A naturally occurring compound or element of a metal found in the earth's crust.
A mineral from which a metal can be extracted profitably and conveniently.
Heating a sulphide ore strongly in the presence of air to convert it into the metal oxide.
Heating a carbonate ore strongly in the absence or limited supply of air to convert it into the metal oxide.
The slow eating away of a metal surface by the action of air, moisture or chemicals around it; rusting of iron is an example.
A homogeneous mixture of a metal with one or more other metals or non-metals, made to improve its properties.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Metals and Non-metals (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) worksheet for Lesson 27 on Metals and Non-metals. Attempt all questions. Write balanced equations in plain text where required.

questions.question: List any four physical properties that distinguish metals from non-metals.
questions.answer:
Four distinguishing physical properties:
1. Lustre: metals are shiny (lustrous); non-metals are generally dull.
2. Malleability/ductility: metals can be beaten into sheets and drawn into wires; non-metals are brittle.
3. Conductivity: metals are good conductors of heat and electricity; non-metals are poor conductors (insulators).
4. Melting point: metals usually have high melting and boiling points; non-metals generally have low ones.
(Metals are also sonorous, whereas non-metals are not.)
questions.explanation: Compare lustre, malleability/ductility, conductivity, sonority and melting point.

questions.question: Name one exception for each: (a) a metal that is liquid at room temperature, (b) a non-metal that conducts electricity, (c) the hardest natural non-metal, (d) a metal soft enough to cut with a knife.
questions.answer:
(a) Mercury - a metal that is liquid at room temperature.
(b) Graphite - a non-metal (form of carbon) that conducts electricity.
(c) Diamond - the hardest natural substance, a non-metal (form of carbon).
(d) Sodium (also potassium) - a metal soft enough to be cut with a knife.
questions.explanation: Standard exceptions to the metal/non-metal property rules.

questions.question: Write balanced equations for the reaction of (a) magnesium with oxygen and (b) zinc with dilute hydrochloric acid. State what kind of oxide is formed in (a).
questions.answer:
(a) 2 Mg + O2 -> 2 MgO. Magnesium oxide (MgO) is a BASIC oxide (it dissolves in water to give an alkali and turns red litmus blue).
(b) Zn + 2 HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2. Zinc displaces hydrogen from the dilute acid, releasing hydrogen gas, because zinc lies above hydrogen in the reactivity series.
questions.explanation: Metal + oxygen gives a basic oxide; metal above H + acid releases H2.

questions.question: Iron nails dipped in copper sulphate solution turn brownish and the blue colour fades. Explain with a balanced equation.
questions.answer:
Iron is more reactive than copper (iron is above copper in the reactivity series), so iron DISPLACES copper from copper sulphate solution:
  Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu
The reddish-brown copper metal deposits on the iron nails (making them brownish), and the blue colour of the copper sulphate solution fades as it changes to pale-green iron sulphate. This is a displacement reaction.
questions.explanation: More reactive iron displaces less reactive copper; colour change confirms it.

questions.question: Define metallurgy. Describe the main steps involved in extracting a metal of medium reactivity (such as zinc) from its ore.
questions.answer:
Metallurgy is the science and process of extracting metals from their ores and refining them for use.
For a medium-reactivity metal such as zinc (obtained from zinc blende, ZnS, or calamine, ZnCO3):
1. Concentration of the ore: earthy impurities (gangue) are removed, for sulphide ores usually by froth flotation.
2. Conversion to the oxide:
   - Roasting (for the sulphide): 2 ZnS + 3 O2 -> 2 ZnO + 2 SO2.
   - Calcination (for the carbonate): ZnCO3 -> ZnO + CO2.
3. Reduction of the oxide to the metal by heating with carbon (coke): ZnO + C -> Zn + CO.
4. Refining: the impure zinc is purified, commonly by electrolytic refining (impure metal as anode, pure metal as cathode).
questions.explanation: Concentration -> roasting/calcination -> reduction with carbon -> refining.

questions.question: Why is aluminium extracted by electrolysis and not by reduction with carbon?
questions.answer: Aluminium is a highly reactive metal (high up in the reactivity series). Its oxide, Al2O3, is very stable and holds onto its oxygen strongly, so carbon is not a strong enough reducing agent to remove the oxygen and free the metal. Therefore aluminium is extracted by ELECTROLYSIS of molten aluminium oxide (the Hall-Heroult process), where electrical energy reduces the aluminium ions to aluminium metal at the cathode. In general, metals high in the reactivity series (Na, Ca, Mg, Al) are obtained by electrolysis of their molten ores.
questions.explanation: Highly reactive metals form very stable oxides that carbon cannot reduce, so electrolysis is used.

questions.question: What is rusting? State the two conditions necessary for the rusting of iron and name two methods of preventing it.
questions.answer:
Rusting is the corrosion of iron, in which iron reacts with oxygen and moisture to form a reddish-brown flaky layer of hydrated iron(III) oxide (Fe2O3.xH2O).
Two conditions necessary for rusting: (1) presence of air (oxygen) and (2) presence of moisture (water). Both must be present together.
Methods of prevention (any two): painting/oiling/greasing the surface; galvanising (coating with zinc); electroplating; or alloying (making stainless steel).
questions.explanation: Rusting needs air + moisture; prevented by painting, galvanising, electroplating, alloying.

questions.question: What is an alloy? Give the composition of brass and bronze, and state one advantage of making alloys.
questions.answer:
An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of a metal with one or more other metals or non-metals.
- Brass = copper + zinc.
- Bronze = copper + tin.
One advantage: alloys are usually harder, stronger and more resistant to corrosion than the pure metal (for example, stainless steel does not rust like pure iron). Alloys may also have a lower melting point or a more attractive appearance.
questions.explanation: Brass = Cu+Zn, bronze = Cu+Sn; alloys improve hardness/strength/corrosion resistance.

questions.question: Arrange the metals K, Cu, Zn, Au and Fe in decreasing order of reactivity. Which of these will NOT react with dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.answer:
Decreasing order of reactivity: K > Zn > Fe > Cu > Au.
Metals below hydrogen in the reactivity series do not displace hydrogen from dilute acids. Copper (Cu) and gold (Au) lie below hydrogen, so they will NOT react with dilute hydrochloric acid. Potassium, zinc and iron (above hydrogen) do react and release hydrogen gas.
questions.explanation: Use the reactivity series; Cu and Au are below hydrogen so do not react with dilute acid.

questions.question: How do the oxides of metals differ from the oxides of non-metals in their acid-base nature? Give one example of each.
questions.answer:
Metal oxides are generally BASIC: they react with acids to form salt and water, and the soluble ones turn red litmus blue. Example: sodium oxide, Na2O (Na2O + H2O -> 2 NaOH).
Non-metal oxides are generally ACIDIC: they react with bases to form salt and water, and the soluble ones turn blue litmus red. Example: carbon dioxide, CO2 (CO2 + H2O -> H2CO3). (Some metal oxides such as Al2O3 and ZnO are amphoteric.)
questions.explanation: Metal oxides basic (e.g. Na2O), non-metal oxides acidic (e.g. CO2).

questions.explanation: Silver (then copper) is the best conductor.

questions.explanation: Ringing sound = sonority (used in bells).

questions.explanation: Non-metals are dull, brittle and poor conductors.

questions.explanation: Wires need conductivity and ductility.

questions.explanation: Bromine is a liquid non-metal (mercury is a liquid metal).

questions.explanation: Foil = thin sheet = malleability.

questions.explanation: Graphite conducts; diamond does not.

questions.explanation: Iodine is lustrous but a non-metal.

questions.explanation: Metal + O2 -> metal oxide.

questions.explanation: Zn + 2 HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2.

questions.explanation: 2 Na + 2 H2O -> 2 NaOH + H2.

questions.question: An oxide that reacts with both acids and bases is called
questions.explanation: E.g. Al2O3 and ZnO.

questions.explanation: CO2 + H2O -> H2CO3 (acidic).

questions.explanation: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series.

questions.question: State three physical properties of metals.
questions.answer: Three physical properties of metals: (1) they are lustrous (shiny); (2) they are malleable and ductile (can be beaten into sheets and drawn into wires); (3) they are good conductors of heat and electricity. (They are also sonorous and have high melting points.)
questions.explanation: Recall lustre, malleability/ductility and conductivity.

questions.question: How do non-metals differ from metals in three physical properties?
questions.answer: Non-metals differ from metals as follows: (1) they are dull (non-lustrous) while metals are shiny; (2) they are brittle (not malleable or ductile) while metals can be hammered and drawn; (3) they are poor conductors of heat and electricity while metals are good conductors. Non-metals also have lower melting points and are not sonorous.
questions.explanation: Dull, brittle, poor conductors versus shiny, malleable, conducting metals.

questions.question: Why are metals used for making cooking utensils and electrical wires?
questions.answer: Metals are used for cooking utensils because they are good conductors of heat (so heat passes quickly to the food), have high melting points (so they do not melt while cooking), and are malleable and strong (so they can be shaped and last long). Metals are used for electrical wires because they are good conductors of electricity and are ductile (so they can be drawn into long thin wires). Copper and aluminium are commonly used for wires.
questions.explanation: Link conductivity, high m.p., malleability/ductility to the uses.

questions.question: Give two exceptions among non-metals with the property that makes each an exception.
questions.answer: Two exceptions among non-metals: (1) Graphite is a non-metal but is a good CONDUCTOR of electricity (most non-metals are insulators). (2) Diamond is a non-metal but is the HARDEST natural substance with a very high melting point (most non-metals are soft and low-melting). Iodine is another exception, being lustrous.
questions.explanation: Graphite conducts; diamond is hardest.

questions.question: Mercury and sodium are both metals, yet they behave unusually. Explain.
questions.answer: Mercury is unusual because, unlike almost all other metals which are solids at room temperature, mercury is a LIQUID at room temperature. Sodium is unusual because it is so SOFT that it can be cut with a knife, whereas most metals are hard and strong. Both are still classed as metals because they show metallic properties such as lustre and conductivity.
questions.explanation: Mercury is a liquid metal; sodium is a soft metal.

questions.question: Write balanced equations for: (a) sodium with water, (b) zinc with sulphuric acid, (c) copper with oxygen.
questions.answer:
(a) 2 Na + 2 H2O -> 2 NaOH + H2 (sodium reacts violently with cold water).
(b) Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2 (zinc displaces hydrogen from the acid).
(c) 2 Cu + O2 -> 2 CuO (copper forms black copper(II) oxide on heating).
questions.explanation: Metal + water -> hydroxide + H2; metal + acid -> salt + H2; metal + O2 -> oxide.

questions.question: Why are metal oxides called basic and non-metal oxides called acidic?
questions.answer: Metal oxides are called basic because they react with acids to form salt and water, and the soluble ones dissolve in water to give alkalis (bases) that turn red litmus blue (e.g. Na2O + H2O -> 2 NaOH). Non-metal oxides are called acidic because they react with bases to form salt and water, and the soluble ones dissolve in water to give acids that turn blue litmus red (e.g. CO2 + H2O -> H2CO3).
questions.explanation: Metal oxides give bases; non-metal oxides give acids in water.

questions.question: Describe, using the example of NaCl, how an ionic bond is formed between a metal and a non-metal.
questions.answer: Sodium (electronic configuration 2,8,1) has one valence electron, which it loses to achieve the stable configuration of neon, becoming a positive ion Na+. Chlorine (2,8,7) needs one electron to complete its octet, so it gains the electron sodium gives up, becoming a negative ion Cl-. The oppositely charged Na+ and Cl- ions attract each other by strong electrostatic force - this attraction is the IONIC (electrovalent) bond, giving sodium chloride, NaCl.
questions.explanation: Metal loses electron(s) -> cation; non-metal gains -> anion; electrostatic attraction is the ionic bond.

questions.question: A student burns sulphur and magnesium separately and tests each oxide with litmus. Predict and explain the results.
questions.answer:
Burning sulphur: S + O2 -> SO2. Sulphur dioxide is a NON-METAL oxide and is acidic; dissolved in water it forms sulphurous acid (SO2 + H2O -> H2SO3), so it turns blue litmus red.
Burning magnesium: 2 Mg + O2 -> 2 MgO. Magnesium oxide is a METAL oxide and is basic; it dissolves slightly to give an alkali, so it turns red litmus blue.
Thus the two oxides have opposite effects on litmus, confirming that non-metal oxides are acidic and metal oxides are basic.
questions.explanation: SO2 acidic (blue->red); MgO basic (red->blue).

questions.question: What is the reactivity series of metals? Write the order for K, Mg, Zn, Cu and Au.
questions.answer: The reactivity series is a list of metals arranged in decreasing order of their chemical reactivity. For the given metals the decreasing order of reactivity is: K > Mg > Zn > Cu > Au. Potassium is the most reactive and gold the least reactive.
questions.explanation: Decreasing reactivity: K > Mg > Zn > Cu > Au.

questions.question: Predict whether each reaction occurs and explain: (a) Zn + CuSO4, (b) Cu + ZnSO4.
questions.answer:
(a) Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu: this reaction OCCURS because zinc is more reactive than copper, so zinc displaces copper from copper sulphate solution (the blue colour fades and copper deposits).
(b) Cu + ZnSO4: NO reaction occurs because copper is less reactive than zinc, and a less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive one from its salt solution.
questions.explanation: Reactive metal displaces less reactive one; reverse does not happen.

questions.question: Why does copper not react with dilute hydrochloric acid while zinc does?
questions.answer: Zinc lies ABOVE hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it can displace hydrogen from dilute acids: Zn + 2 HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2. Copper lies BELOW hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it is less reactive than hydrogen and cannot displace it from the acid; hence copper does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid.
questions.explanation: Zn above H reacts; Cu below H does not.

questions.question: Metal A displaces B from its salt solution; B displaces C; C does not displace A. Arrange A, B and C in order of reactivity and justify.
questions.answer:
Order of decreasing reactivity: A > B > C.
Justification: A displaces B, so A is more reactive than B. B displaces C, so B is more reactive than C. C does not displace A, which is consistent with A being the most reactive (a less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive one). Combining these gives A > B > C.
questions.explanation: Displacement shows the displacing metal is more reactive.

questions.question: What is a displacement reaction? Give one example with a balanced equation.
questions.answer:
A displacement reaction is one in which a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution (or compound). Example: iron is more reactive than copper, so:
  Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu
Here iron displaces copper from copper sulphate solution.
questions.explanation: Definition plus Fe + CuSO4 example.

questions.question: Define the terms 'mineral' and 'ore'.
questions.answer: A mineral is a naturally occurring substance (element or compound of a metal) found in the earth's crust. An ore is a mineral from which a metal can be extracted profitably and conveniently. Thus all ores are minerals, but not all minerals are ores.
questions.explanation: Mineral = natural source; ore = profitably workable mineral.

questions.question: List, in order, the four main steps in the extraction of a metal from its ore.
questions.answer:
The four main steps are:
1. Concentration (enrichment) of the ore - removing earthy impurities (gangue), e.g. by washing, magnetic separation or froth flotation.
2. Conversion of the concentrated ore to its oxide - by roasting (sulphides) or calcination (carbonates).
3. Reduction of the oxide to the free metal - using carbon for medium-reactivity metals or electrolysis for highly reactive ones.
4. Refining (purification) of the metal - commonly by electrolytic refining.
questions.explanation: Concentration -> conversion to oxide -> reduction -> refining.

questions.question: Differentiate between roasting and calcination with one equation each.
questions.answer:
Roasting is the strong heating of a SULPHIDE ore in the PRESENCE of air to convert it to the oxide: 2 ZnS + 3 O2 -> 2 ZnO + 2 SO2.
Calcination is the strong heating of a CARBONATE ore in the ABSENCE (or limited supply) of air to convert it to the oxide: ZnCO3 -> ZnO + CO2.
questions.explanation: Roasting: sulphide + air; calcination: carbonate without air.

questions.question: Describe electrolytic refining of an impure metal such as copper.
questions.answer: In electrolytic refining, a block of the impure metal is made the ANODE and a thin strip of pure metal the CATHODE, both dipped in a solution of a salt of the metal (e.g. copper sulphate for copper) as electrolyte. When current is passed, the impure metal at the anode dissolves into the solution and pure metal is deposited on the cathode. The soluble impurities stay in solution and the insoluble impurities settle below the anode as 'anode mud'. This gives a very pure metal.
questions.explanation: Impure metal anode, pure cathode, salt electrolyte; pure metal deposits on cathode.

questions.question: How are metals of low reactivity such as gold and silver obtained?
questions.answer: Metals of low reactivity such as gold and silver are very unreactive, so they often occur in the FREE (native) state in nature and need little chemical treatment. Where they occur as compounds (e.g. some silver and mercury ores), they can be obtained simply by heating the ore (for example, heating mercury(II) oxide: 2 HgO -> 2 Hg + O2), as their oxides decompose easily on heating.
questions.explanation: Low-reactivity metals occur native or are obtained by simple heating.

questions.question: Explain why sodium is extracted by electrolysis but iron is extracted by reduction with carbon.
questions.answer:
Sodium is very high in the reactivity series and forms an extremely stable compound (e.g. NaCl). Carbon is not a strong enough reducing agent to free such a reactive metal, so sodium is obtained by ELECTROLYSIS of molten sodium chloride, where electricity reduces Na+ ions to sodium metal.
Iron is only a medium-reactivity metal; its oxide is far less stable, so it CAN be reduced cheaply by carbon (or carbon monoxide) in a blast furnace: Fe2O3 + 3 CO -> 2 Fe + 3 CO2. Hence the extraction method depends on the metal's position in the reactivity series.
questions.explanation: High reactivity -> electrolysis; medium reactivity -> reduction by carbon.

questions.question: Write the equations for the reduction of zinc oxide and iron(III) oxide using carbon-based reducing agents.
questions.answer:
Zinc oxide reduced by carbon: ZnO + C -> Zn + CO.
Iron(III) oxide reduced by carbon monoxide (in the blast furnace): Fe2O3 + 3 CO -> 2 Fe + 3 CO2.
In both cases the oxide loses oxygen (is reduced) and the metal is set free.
questions.explanation: ZnO + C -> Zn + CO; Fe2O3 + 3 CO -> 2 Fe + 3 CO2.

questions.question: What is corrosion? Give one example other than rusting.
questions.answer: Corrosion is the slow eating away of the surface of a metal by the action of air, moisture or chemicals around it. An example other than rusting is the tarnishing of silver, in which silver forms a black coating of silver sulphide; another is the green coating (basic copper carbonate) that forms on copper articles.
questions.explanation: Corrosion = slow eating away of metal; e.g. silver tarnishing or copper turning green.

questions.question: State the conditions for rusting of iron and describe an experiment that proves both air and water are needed.
questions.answer: Rusting needs BOTH air (oxygen) and moisture (water). Experiment: take three test tubes each with an iron nail. (1) In the first, add water that has been boiled (to remove dissolved air) and cover it with oil to keep air out. (2) In the second, add anhydrous calcium chloride (a drying agent) and seal it so the air is dry. (3) In the third, keep the nail in ordinary water exposed to air. After a few days only the nail in the third tube (with both air and water) rusts, while the nails in the first (no air) and second (no moisture) do not. This proves both air and water are necessary.
questions.explanation: Three-tube experiment: only the nail with both air and water rusts.

questions.question: Describe three methods of preventing the corrosion of iron.
questions.answer: Three methods of preventing corrosion of iron: (1) Painting, oiling or greasing the surface forms a barrier that keeps out air and moisture. (2) Galvanising - coating the iron with a layer of zinc; zinc protects the iron because it is more reactive and corrodes in preference to iron, and the coating also keeps out air/moisture. (3) Alloying - converting iron into stainless steel (iron + chromium + nickel), which does not rust. Electroplating with chromium, tin or nickel also prevents corrosion.
questions.explanation: Painting/oiling, galvanising, alloying (and electroplating).

questions.question: Why does galvanising protect iron even if the zinc layer is scratched?
questions.answer: Zinc is MORE reactive than iron. Even if the zinc coating is scratched and the iron underneath is exposed to air and moisture, the zinc corrodes in preference to the iron (it acts as a sacrificial metal), so the iron is protected from rusting until the zinc is used up. This is why galvanising gives better protection than an ordinary coating that only acts as a physical barrier.
questions.explanation: Zinc is more reactive and corrodes sacrificially, protecting the iron.

questions.question: What is an alloy? Give two examples with their composition.
questions.answer: An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of a metal with one or more other metals or non-metals. Examples: (1) Brass = copper + zinc; (2) Bronze = copper + tin. (Other examples include steel = iron + carbon and solder = lead + tin.)
questions.explanation: Definition plus brass (Cu+Zn) and bronze (Cu+Sn).

questions.question: State the composition and one use each of stainless steel, solder and amalgam.
questions.answer: Stainless steel: iron + chromium + nickel (with a little carbon); used for cutlery, utensils and surgical instruments because it does not rust. Solder: lead + tin; has a low melting point and is used for joining (soldering) electrical wires and metal parts. Amalgam: an alloy of mercury with another metal; dental amalgam is used to fill teeth.
questions.explanation: Stainless steel (Fe+Cr+Ni), solder (Pb+Sn), amalgam (with Hg) with uses.

questions.question: Give two reasons why alloys are preferred over pure metals.
questions.answer: Alloys are preferred because: (1) they are usually harder and stronger than the pure metal (e.g. steel is much harder than pure iron), and (2) they are more resistant to corrosion (e.g. stainless steel does not rust). Alloys may also have a lower melting point (useful for solder) or a more attractive appearance.
questions.explanation: Greater hardness/strength and corrosion resistance.

questions.question: Pure gold (24 carat) is rarely used to make jewellery. Explain why an alloy is used instead.
questions.answer: Pure gold (24 carat) is very SOFT, so jewellery made from it would bend, scratch and lose its shape easily. To make it harder and more durable, gold is alloyed with a small amount of another metal such as copper or silver (giving, for example, 22 carat gold). The alloy keeps the attractive golden appearance but is much stronger and more hard-wearing, so it is better suited for ornaments.
questions.explanation: Pure gold is too soft; alloying with Cu/Ag makes durable jewellery.

questions.question: What are metalloids? Give two examples and state how they relate to metals and non-metals.
questions.answer: Metalloids are elements that show properties INTERMEDIATE between metals and non-metals - that is, some properties of each. Two examples are silicon and germanium. They lie along the borderline of the metals and non-metals in the periodic table and are widely used as semiconductors in electronic devices.
questions.explanation: Metalloids show properties of both; e.g. silicon and germanium (semiconductors).

questions.question: A teacher shows students four samples: a shiny wire that bends easily and conducts electricity, a brittle yellow solid that does not conduct, a silvery liquid, and a black solid that conducts electricity. Answer: (a) Which sample is most likely a typical metal and why? (b) Which is most likely a typical non-metal? (c) Identify the silvery liquid and say whether it is a metal or non-metal. (d) Name the conducting black solid that is actually a non-metal.
questions.answer: (a) The shiny wire that bends easily and conducts electricity is a typical METAL - it shows lustre, malleability/ductility and conductivity. (b) The brittle yellow solid that does not conduct is a typical NON-METAL (such as sulphur) - dull, brittle and an insulator. (c) The silvery liquid is MERCURY, which is a METAL (the only common metal that is liquid at room temperature). (d) The conducting black solid that is a non-metal is GRAPHITE (a form of carbon).
questions.explanation: Identify metal (shiny, ductile, conducting), non-metal (brittle, insulating), mercury (liquid metal) and graphite (conducting non-metal).

questions.question: Carbon exists in two well-known forms: diamond and graphite. Diamond is the hardest known substance and does not conduct electricity, while graphite is soft, slippery and conducts electricity. Answer: (a) Are diamond and graphite metals or non-metals? (b) Which one is used in electrodes and why? (c) Which is used in cutting tools and why? (d) Why are these considered 'exceptions'?
questions.answer: (a) Both diamond and graphite are NON-METALS - they are different forms (allotropes) of the element carbon. (b) Graphite is used in electrodes because it CONDUCTS electricity (unusual for a non-metal). (c) Diamond is used in cutting and drilling tools because it is the HARDEST known substance. (d) They are exceptions because graphite conducts electricity (most non-metals are insulators) and diamond is extremely hard with a very high melting point (most non-metals are soft and low-melting).
questions.explanation: Both non-metals; graphite conducts (electrodes), diamond is hardest (cutting); exceptions to non-metal rules.

questions.question: Magnesium ribbon is burnt in air. A bright white flame is seen and a white powder is formed. The white powder is dissolved in water and tested with litmus. Answer: (a) Write the balanced equation for the burning of magnesium. (b) Name the white powder. (c) Is the powder's solution acidic or basic, and what is the litmus result? (d) What general rule about metal oxides does this illustrate?
questions.answer: (a) 2 Mg + O2 -> 2 MgO. (b) The white powder is magnesium oxide (MgO). (c) MgO dissolves slightly in water to form magnesium hydroxide, which is BASIC (alkaline); it turns red litmus blue. (d) This illustrates the general rule that the oxides of METALS are basic in nature (whereas the oxides of non-metals are acidic).
questions.explanation: Mg + O2 -> MgO; MgO is basic, turns red litmus blue; metal oxides are basic.

questions.question: Four metals P, Q, R and S are tested. P displaces Q, R and S from their salt solutions. S does not displace any of the others. Q displaces R and S but not P. R displaces only S. Answer: (a) Arrange P, Q, R and S in decreasing order of reactivity. (b) Which is the most reactive? (c) Which is the least reactive? (d) Will R displace Q from its salt solution? Explain.
questions.answer:
Analyse the displacements: P displaces Q, R, S (most reactive); Q displaces R and S but not P; R displaces only S; S displaces none (least reactive).
(a) Decreasing order of reactivity: P > Q > R > S. (b) The most reactive is P. (c) The least reactive is S. (d) R will NOT displace Q, because Q is more reactive than R, and a less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive one from its salt solution.
questions.explanation: Order P>Q>R>S; P most, S least reactive; R cannot displace the more reactive Q.

questions.question: An iron knife is left dipped in a blue copper sulphate solution for some time. After a while the knife is coated with a reddish-brown layer and the blue solution turns pale green. Answer: (a) What type of reaction has taken place? (b) Write the balanced equation. (c) Why does the blue colour fade? (d) Why does copper not show a similar reaction when dipped in iron sulphate?
questions.answer: (a) A DISPLACEMENT reaction has taken place. (b) Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu. (c) The blue colour of copper sulphate fades because copper ions (blue) are removed from solution as copper metal deposits on the knife, and pale-green iron sulphate forms instead. (d) Copper is less reactive than iron, so copper cannot displace iron from iron sulphate solution; hence no reaction occurs.
questions.explanation: Displacement Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu; blue fades as Cu deposits; Cu cannot displace more reactive Fe.

questions.question: Zinc is obtained from its main ore, zinc blende (ZnS). Answer: (a) What is the difference between a mineral and an ore? (b) Which process converts ZnS to ZnO and what is it called? (c) Write the equation for the reduction of ZnO to zinc metal. (d) Name the method commonly used to purify the impure zinc.
questions.answer: (a) A mineral is any naturally occurring compound/element of a metal; an ore is a mineral from which the metal can be extracted profitably. (b) ZnS is heated strongly in air, converting it to ZnO; this process is called ROASTING: 2 ZnS + 3 O2 -> 2 ZnO + 2 SO2. (c) Reduction of zinc oxide with carbon: ZnO + C -> Zn + CO. (d) The impure zinc is commonly purified by electrolytic refining.
questions.explanation: Mineral vs ore; roasting of ZnS; ZnO + C -> Zn + CO; electrolytic refining.

questions.question: Three metals - sodium, iron and gold - are to be extracted. Sodium is highly reactive, iron is of medium reactivity, and gold is very unreactive. Answer: (a) Which extraction method suits sodium and why? (b) How is iron extracted from its oxide ore? (c) How is gold usually obtained? (d) What property decides the method used?
questions.answer: (a) Sodium is highly reactive and forms a very stable compound, so it is extracted by ELECTROLYSIS of molten sodium chloride - carbon cannot reduce such a reactive metal. (b) Iron, a medium-reactivity metal, is extracted by reducing its oxide with carbon/carbon monoxide in a blast furnace: Fe2O3 + 3 CO -> 2 Fe + 3 CO2. (c) Gold is very unreactive, so it usually occurs in the free (native) state and is obtained with little chemical treatment. (d) The position of the metal in the REACTIVITY SERIES decides the method used.
questions.explanation: Na - electrolysis; Fe - reduction with carbon; Au - found native; reactivity series decides method.

questions.question: An iron gate left exposed to rain and air develops a flaky reddish-brown layer over several weeks. The owner wants to prevent this. Answer: (a) Name the process occurring. (b) What two conditions caused it? (c) Name the substance formed. (d) Suggest two practical ways the owner can prevent it.
questions.answer: (a) The process is RUSTING (a form of corrosion). (b) It was caused by the presence of BOTH air (oxygen) and moisture (rain water). (c) The substance formed is rust - hydrated iron(III) oxide (Fe2O3.xH2O). (d) The owner can prevent it by painting the gate (a barrier against air and moisture) and by galvanising it (coating with zinc); oiling/greasing or using stainless steel are other options.
questions.explanation: Rusting; air + moisture; hydrated iron(III) oxide; prevent by painting and galvanising.

questions.question: A manufacturer needs materials for: utensils that must not rust, electrical wires that must be soldered, and decorative door handles. Answer: (a) Which alloy is suitable for rust-free utensils and what is its composition? (b) Which alloy is used to solder the wires and why? (c) Which alloy gives attractive, lustrous door handles? (d) Give one general advantage of using alloys.
questions.answer: (a) Stainless steel (iron + chromium + nickel, with a little carbon) is suitable for rust-free utensils because it resists corrosion. (b) Solder (lead + tin) is used to join the wires because it has a low melting point and joins metals easily. (c) Brass (copper + zinc) gives attractive, lustrous door handles. (d) A general advantage: alloys are harder, stronger and more corrosion-resistant (or more attractive) than the pure metals.
questions.explanation: Stainless steel (Fe+Cr+Ni); solder (Pb+Sn, low m.p.); brass (Cu+Zn); alloys are harder/stronger/corrosion-resistant.

questions.question: Two test tubes are taken: one contains dilute hydrochloric acid with a piece of zinc, the other the same acid with a piece of copper. Bubbles of gas appear only in the zinc tube. Answer: (a) Name the gas evolved. (b) Write the equation for the reaction that occurs. (c) Why does no reaction occur in the copper tube? (d) How could you test the gas evolved?
questions.answer: (a) The gas evolved is hydrogen. (b) Zn + 2 HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2. (c) No reaction occurs in the copper tube because copper lies below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from the dilute acid. (d) The gas can be tested by bringing a burning splint near the mouth of the tube - hydrogen burns with a 'pop' sound.
questions.explanation: Hydrogen from Zn + HCl; Cu below H so no reaction; test H2 with the pop test.
